title: The restless mind
hook: Arjuna says the mind is restless as the wind; Krishna: practice and detachment tame it (Bhagavad Gita 6.34–35)
tomorrow: what are the seven verses said in every Muslim prayer?

segments.voice: Yesterday, moderate in all: a seat not too high and not too low, and a life measured the same way. Moderate.

Ten seconds into a meditation app, and the mind is already planning dinner. There's company for that in an old place. In chapter six, after Krishna has described the seat and the steady mind, Arjuna pushes back. This evenness you teach, he says, I can't see how it lasts. The mind is restless, turbulent, strong and stubborn. Holding it seems as hard as holding the wind.
screen: `TEN SECONDS IN, PLANNING DINNER.` → `ARJUNA PUSHES BACK.` → `AS HARD TO HOLD AS THE WIND.`

segments.voice: Two sides, and the Gita lets both speak. Arjuna's case is strong. He isn't lazy; he's honest. He has watched his own mind, and it moves like weather. A teaching that only works for a calm mind, he's saying, doesn't help the person who needs it most. Krishna doesn't fight that. His first word is a concession: doubtless, the mind is restless and hard to hold. Then his answer: it is held by practice, and by letting go. The Sanskrit pair is abhyasa and vairagya. Abhyasa is coming back to the same place, again and again; a few verses earlier Krishna says, wherever the restless mind wanders, bring it back. Vairagya is loosening the grip of wanting, so there's less pulling the mind away. Then Krishna keeps Arjuna's point alive: for one without self-control, he says, this yoga is hard to reach; for the one who keeps striving by the right means, it can be reached. So who wins? In the text, neither side is erased. Arjuna names a problem nobody can wave away; Krishna names the slow road through it. And one more thread: the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, a separate Hindu text on stilling the mind, use the very same pair.
screen: `ARJUNA: THE MIND IS WIND.` · `KRISHNA: DOUBTLESS. AND YET.` · `ABHYASA AND VAIRAGYA.` · `PATANJALI USES THE SAME PAIR.` · then, large: `PRACTICE AND LETTING GO.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and rest your attention on the breath where it enters the nose. When the mind wanders, and it will, that's the practice: notice it, let the thought go without chasing it, and come back. Every return counts.
The restless mind: Arjuna's wind, and Krishna's two-handed answer, abhyasa and vairagya.
Hold on to this: practice and letting go, both hands on the wind. That's the Gita, six of six.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers of meditation draw on Gita 6.35 and on Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, where practice and letting go are named together as the way the mind is stilled.

chat.meaning: Krishna grants that the mind is restless, then names two hands: abhyasa, coming back again and again, and vairagya, loosening the grip.

abhyasa.meaning: Sanskrit: practice, coming back again and again

vairagya.meaning: Sanskrit: letting go, loosening the grip of wanting

Patanjali.meaning: the sage named as author of the Yoga Sutras

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 6.33–34 (Arjuna: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, as hard to control as the wind)

Bhagavad Gita 6.35–36 (Krishna: doubtless the mind is restless and hard to hold, but it is held by practice and dispassion; hard for the uncontrolled, attainable for the one who strives by right means)
Bhagavad Gita 6.26 (wherever the restless mind wanders, bring it back)
Patanjali, Yoga Sutras 1.12 (the stilling of the mind comes by practice and non-attachment, abhyasa and vairagya)
